name: Scarcity
statement: Things in short supply, and things that have just become short, are rated as more desirable and more valuable than the same things in plentiful supply.
meaning: The claim is about how an object is valued, not about the psychology of being poor. Brock's commodity theory puts it generally, and Lynn quotes the central sentence from page 246: any commodity will be valued to the extent that it is unavailable. Marketing research splits the cue into three kinds. Supply-based scarcity restricts how many exist, demand-based scarcity signals that other buyers have taken them, and time-based scarcity closes the window for buying. The three travel under one name and do not behave alike. Reactance, entry 86 here, is one candidate explanation for the effect rather than the effect itself. The resource-scarcity literature, entry 422, is a different subject with a different record.

origin.note: Brock's chapter set out commodity theory, of which the scarcity effect is the best known prediction. The demonstration usually cited is seven years later, Worchel, Lee and Adewole's cookie experiment of 1975. The route into marketing practice runs through Cialdini's Influence, which both meta-analyses below cite for the claim itself rather than for evidence.

evidence: The cookie experiment is described here from its abstract, because no open copy of the paper exists. Across two experiments 200 female undergraduates rated the value and attractiveness of cookies held either in abundant or in scarce supply. Supply was either constant or changing, and a change was attributed either to an accident or to demand from other participants. These conditions were crossed with what participants believed about how many more people were still to take part. Cookies in scarce supply were rated as more desirable than cookies in abundant supply. Cookies whose supply fell from abundant to scarce were rated as more valuable than cookies that had been scarce throughout, and cookies scarce through demand beat cookies scarce through an accident. The abstract carries a fourth result the retellings drop: among the abundant conditions, constantly abundant cookies were rated higher than cookies that began scarce and later became abundant. The authors read the results as an extension of commodity theory and hypothesised reactance as an intervening process behind some of them. A second study was run to rule out demand characteristics. The 200 is the combined total for both experiments, and it is the only number from that paper quoted here. No mean or test statistic from it appears on this page. Lynn pooled the first two decades of the literature: 41 studies containing 51 tests of the scarcity principle, combined by the Stouffer method to z = 8.39. The mean effect size was r = 0.12, rising to 0.17 once five significant reversals were dropped as outliers, and individual effects ran from -0.54 to 0.43 with significant heterogeneity, chi-squared(48) = 190.22, p < 0.005. Tests of the uniqueness explanation gave a combined z = 3.59 while reaching significance in only 4 of 11 tests.

examples.text: A shop puts a card on the shelf saying a biscuit is being dropped and this is the last of the stock. Regulars who bought a packet a month buy four, and describe the biscuit as better than they had remembered. Nothing about the biscuit changed.

examples.tag: Two places left on the sign-up
examples.text: A talk at the library sits half booked for a fortnight and stirs nobody. The sign-up page then reads two places left, and both go within the hour to people who had passed it over. The shortage, not the speaker, did the persuading.

examples.tag: The allotment with a waiting list
examples.text: Plots on the site with the four-year waiting list are spoken of as the good ground, by people who have never dug either site. Unavailability is being read as a report on quality, which is the whole of the effect and not much of it.

replication.headline: Two meta-analyses thirty years apart both find a positive pooled effect, and the modern one puts it at 0.31 on purchase intentions across 193 effect sizes.
replication.detail: Barton, Zlatevska and Oppewal pooled 416 effect sizes from 131 studies published over 50 years. For purchase intentions they report 193 effect sizes covering 22,655 participants at 0.31, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.37, z = 10.01. Their metric is a reliability-corrected, inverse-variance-weighted standardised mean difference rather than a plain Cohen's d. The same pooling gives attitude 0.15, desirability 0.25, enjoyment 0.33, perceived value 0.37, perceived quality 0.47, willingness to pay 0.47, exclusivity 0.52 and popularity 0.71. Ladeira and colleagues pooled 335 effect sizes from 37 articles and report a mean of 0.2776, printed with a 95% interval of 0.2243 to 0.3209, z = 11.06, with I-squared of 68% and chi-squared(224) = 875.83. The two disagree about which cue does the work. Barton's three-way comparison put supply-based scarcity largest at 0.39, time-based at 0.34 and demand-based at 0.28, a spread that did not reach significance, Q(2) = 1.76, p = .414. That aggregate is not their conclusion, and the page should not be read as though it were. Barton's abstract says instead that demand-based scarcity works best for utilitarian products, supply-based for experiences and time-based for high-involvement products. Within hedonic products the sources did differ, Q(2) = 9.63, with supply at 0.55 against demand at 0.17. Within utilitarian products the ordering reversed, Q(2) = 12.38, with demand at 0.41 against supply at -0.02 and time at 0.02. Ladeira ran a different contrast and called it significant: excessive demand 0.5484 from 58 effects, 95% CI 0.4412 to 0.6557, against restricted supply 0.1859 from 107 effects, 95% CI 0.1362 to 0.2355, with a metaregression coefficient of -0.346, standard error 0.054, p < 0.001. They agree only on limited quantity against limited time. Ladeira gives limited quantity 0.287 and limited time 0.3952 from 51 effects, with a coefficient of 0.1030, standard error 0.0649, whose interval includes zero.

study.cite: Barton, B. L., Zlatevska, N., & Oppewal, H. (2022). Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions. Journal of Retailing, 98(4), 741-758.

limits: Almost all of this is an intention recorded in a scenario. Of Barton's 193 purchase-intention effect sizes, 178 came from hypothetical manipulations and 15 from actual ones, and 152 of them came from student samples. Neither contrast reached significance, Q(1) = 0.08 for manipulation type and Q(1) = 1.56 for sample composition, so the small real-behaviour set does not contradict the rest. Across the whole Barton dataset the position is starker. They record only 24 effect sizes measuring actual behaviour and only 6 from field-based studies, against 384 hypothetical ones. Their own list of open questions asks under what conditions purchase intentions translate into actual purchases. Lynn made the same complaint in 1991, writing that little research to date had used these manipulations in real-world marketing contexts. Publication bias is handled in both papers by a fail-safe count and nothing else. Barton write that their analysis did not include unpublished studies, and that between 30 and 6,985 studies would be required to reduce the significant results to non-significance. Lynn's equivalent figure was 1,277. Effects differ by country in Barton's data at Q(5) = 10.33, p = .066, with Korea at 0.70 and Canada at 0.49 against Germany at 0.05 and the Netherlands at 0.19, the last two not significant. Lynn declined to interpret his own moderators, on the grounds that the study characteristics he coded were highly correlated and that different but equally defensible inclusion decisions changed the answers. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and general web search on 21 September 2026 found no preregistered or multi-laboratory direct replication of the 1975 cookie experiment, so the case rests on meta-analytic accumulation of conceptual replications. That paper could not be obtained here. Unpaywall records no open copy, APA PsycNet returned a script shell behind an Imperva bot check rather than a record, and Ovid redirected the article to a Wolters Kluwer sign-in. None of those is a paywall notice, and the abstract was read instead at Ovid's public record and at OpenAlex.
misreadings: The loudest confusion is with a different literature. Mullainathan and Shafir's work on the scarcity of money and time asks what having too little does to attention and decision-making, which is not a claim about what a limited edition does to a product's appeal. That body of work has its own entry here, number 422, and its own contested record. Its numbers are deliberately not repeated on this page. O'Donnell and colleagues' audit of it was corrected by its authors in 2022 and answered by two comments in 2023, so any figure lifted from the 2021 text without that history is already out of date. Isler, Yilmaz and Dulleck belong to that literature too. Their preregistered experiment of 3,442 participants is a direct replication of Shah, Shafir and Mullainathan's claim that scarcity frames value, and its title makes the support conditional: scarcity improves valuations when cognitively salient. The published abstract reports that the effects only tended to be smaller among those facing higher income scarcity. The article itself could not be opened here, so nothing stronger than that is claimed. Reactance is a hypothesis about scarcity rather than a finding about it, and entry 86 carries its record. Worchel and colleagues offered it as an intervening process behind some of their results. Barton and colleagues treat commodity theory as the dominant framework, list conformity, regret and reactance as alternatives, and say their meta-analysis could not code variables belonging to those frameworks because too few studies measured them. Lynn notes that reactance predicts a scarcity effect only where a person treats possession as a right or a freedom, which is narrower than what commodity theory claims. A third error is that limited-time appeals beat limited-quantity appeals, or the reverse. Both meta-analyses looked at that particular pair and found nothing. Neither result licenses the wider claim that the three cues are interchangeable, which both papers contradict. Possession is a separate matter from scarcity, and the endowment effect at entry 46 covers it. Lynn coded whether participants held the commodity before rating it, and found the scarcity effect reliable for possessed and unpossessed commodities alike. Scarcity also does not always raise value. Five of the 51 tests in Lynn's set reversed significantly, three of them in studies where participants ranked commodities they believed would then be handed out, a setting in which naming the scarce one looks selfish. Last, the effect is smaller than the anecdotes imply. Lynn's mean r of 0.12 accounts for about 1% of the variance, which he renders as a success rate moving from 44% to 56%.

sources.text: Brock, T. C. (1968). Implications of commodity theory for value change. In Psychological Foundations of Attitudes (pp. 243-275). Academic Press. The chapter was not read; its central claim is quoted on this page from Lynn (1991).

Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906-914. No full text obtained. Unpaywall records no open copy, APA PsycNet served a script shell behind an Imperva bot check, and Ovid's full-text view redirected to a Wolters Kluwer sign-in. Described here from the PsycINFO abstract on Ovid's public record, cross-checked against the abstract in OpenAlex.
Lynn, M. (1991). Scarcity effects on value: A quantitative review of the commodity theory literature. Psychology & Marketing, 8(1), 43-57. Read from the author copy at Cornell eCommons.

Barton, B. L., Zlatevska, N., & Oppewal, H. (2022). Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions. Journal of Retailing, 98(4), 741-758. Read from the accepted version in the Bond University repository.

Ladeira, W. J., Lim, W. M., Santini, F. de O., Rasul, T., Perin, M. G., & Altinay, L. (2023). A meta-analysis on the effects of product scarcity. Psychology & Marketing, 40(7), 1267-1279. Read from the copy in the Oxford Brookes RADAR repository.

O'Donnell, M., et al. (2021). Empirical audit and review and an assessment of evidentiary value in research on the psychological consequences of scarcity. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118(44), e2103313118. Read in full at Europe PMC, which still carries the uncorrected 2021 text. Cited for the resource-scarcity literature, which is not the effect described on this page. Entry 422 carries its figures.

Correction for O'Donnell et al., Empirical audit and review and an assessment of evidentiary value in research on the psychological consequences of scarcity (2022). Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(48), e2217321119. Read in full. It removes one replication and records that 18, not 20, of the replicated effects were significant when first published.

Isler, O., Yilmaz, O., & Dulleck, U. (2023). Scarcity improves economic valuations when cognitively salient. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 209, 362-371. Full text not obtained on 21 September 2026. ScienceDirect and the publisher DOI answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge, the University of Canberra copy of the publisher PDF and the CEPR copy were both blocked by Cloudflare, web.archive.org was unreachable, and the authors' OSF deposit holds data, code and instructions but no manuscript. The QUT ePrints record holds no file and points to the publisher; its publisher abstract was read there.

Cialdini, R. B. Influence. Named as the route by which scarcity reached marketing practice, cited by Lynn (1991) as the 1985 edition and by Barton and colleagues (2022) as the 2009 edition. The book was not read and no claim on this page rests on it.
